country.name: Lebanon
country.tagline: Phoenician wine, Roman temples and Jesuit cellars, made every vintage through war in the high Bekaa.

stats.note: Wine-grape area approximate (roughly 2,000 to 3,000 ha of wine grapes; total vineyard including table grapes is larger). Lebanese wineries produced about 15 million bottles in 2024 despite the war, per press reports cited on Wikipedia; the Union Vinicole du Liban has estimated around 9 million bottles in normal years.

country.overview:
Lebanon is the coast that taught the Mediterranean to trade wine. Phoenician ports at Byblos, Tyre and Sidon shipped wine to Old Kingdom Egypt, and Phoenician sailors carried vines and amphorae to Carthage, Sicily, Sardinia and Spain; a seventh-century BC wine press at Tell el-Burak near Sidon shows production for export. The prophet Hosea compared Israel's future fame to 'the wine of Lebanon'. Under Rome, the great sanctuary at Baalbek in the Bekaa included the Temple of Bacchus, one of the best-preserved Roman temples anywhere, its doorway carved with vines and grapes.

Four centuries of Ottoman rule kept commercial wine to Christian communities making it for the church. The modern revival began in the Bekaa in the mid-nineteenth century: Château Ksara was founded by Jesuits in 1857 near Zahlé, and in 1898 they found the Roman-era caves that are now its cellar; Domaine des Tourelles followed in 1868. The French Mandate created a market for wine in Beirut, and in 1930 Gaston Hochar founded Château Musar at Ghazir, north of Beirut. His son Serge, Bordeaux-trained under Émile Peynaud, made Musar from 1959 until his death in 2014 and turned it into one of the cult wines of the world after Michael Broadbent picked the 1967 at the Bristol Wine Fair of 1979.

The legend of Lebanese wine is resilience. Through the civil war of 1975 to 1990, Musar missed only one vintage (1976); in 1982 its Bekaa vineyards lay on the front line between Syrian and Israeli tanks; in 2006 and again in 2024 harvests went on under airstrikes. Since the 1990s the number of wineries has grown from a handful to around 50 to 60, with Kefraya, Massaya, Ixsir, Domaine Wardy, Château Marsyas, Atibaia and many small producers. Most vineyards are in the Bekaa at about 900 to 1,200 metres, between the Mount Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, with newer high vineyards in Batroun, Jezzine and Mount Lebanon.

Two native white grapes, Obaideh and Merwah, give Lebanon its own voice (they are the white in Château Musar Blanc), and producers are reviving others such as Zeini, Meksassi, Asmi Noir and Sabbagieh. Reds are mostly Cinsault, Carignan, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Grenache and Mourvèdre, with a warm, spicy character from sun and altitude.

history.title: Byblos wine for the pharaohs
history.text: Wine from Byblos and the Phoenician coast was shipped to Old Kingdom Egypt, one of the earliest long-distance wine trades.

history.title: The wine press of Tell el-Burak
history.text: Excavations near Sidon found a large plastered Phoenician wine press with vineyards nearby, built to produce wine for overseas trade.

history.title: The Temple of Bacchus at Baalbek
history.text: Rome built the Temple of Bacchus within the sanctuary of Heliopolis in the Bekaa, its stone carved with vines, grapes and drinking scenes.

history.title: Jesuits found Château Ksara
history.text: Jesuit priests planted vines at Ksara near Zahlé; in 1898 they found Roman-era caves, now two kilometres of cellars.

history.title: Gaston Hochar founds Château Musar
history.text: Hochar, back from Bordeaux, set up Musar in an eighteenth-century castle at Ghazir; his son Serge took over winemaking in 1959.

history.title: Musar discovered at Bristol
history.text: Michael Broadbent named the 1967 Château Musar the discovery of the Bristol Wine Fair, opening the UK market.

history.title: Vintages through civil war
history.text: Lebanese wineries kept harvesting through the civil war; Musar missed only 1976.

history.title: Harvest under fire
history.text: Israeli strikes hit the Bekaa during the 2024 war; producers still harvested and bottled around 15 million bottles.

country.classification: Lebanon has no appellation system. It joined the OIV in 1996, and the producers' association Union Vinicole du Liban, founded in 1997, promotes common standards and exports; labels carry winery names and broad regions (Bekaa Valley, Batroun, Mount Lebanon) rather than regulated appellations.
country.climate_soils: The Bekaa is a high plain at 900 to 1,200 metres between two ranges over 2,000 metres high: hot, dry summers with no rain from May to October, cold nights, snowy winters and snowmelt groundwater. Soils are limestone, clay and gravel, red in places. Coastal and Mount Lebanon vineyards (Batroun, Jezzine, Kesrouan) climb to 1,400 metres and more, with more maritime influence.

grapes.name: Obaideh
grapes.note: Native white, rich and creamy with low acidity, sometimes said to be related to Chardonnay (not confirmed); in Musar Blanc.

grapes.name: Merwah
grapes.note: Native white from Mount Lebanon, often linked to Sémillon; fresh and nutty.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.note: Planted by the Jesuits; the traditional red base of the Bekaa.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Carignan, Grenache, Mourvèdre

further_reading: Arak and Mezze: The Taste of Lebanon, Michael Karam

regions.name: Bekaa Valley
regions.tagline: A high plain between two mountain ranges, home of almost all Lebanese wine.
regions.summary: The Bekaa produces most of Lebanon's wine, concentrated in the central and western valley around Zahlé, Chtaura, Kefraya, Tanail and the West Bekaa, with Baalbek's Roman temple at the northern end. Ksara, Kefraya, Musar's vineyards, Massaya, Domaine des Tourelles, Domaine Wardy and Château Marsyas are here.
regions.history: Supplied the Phoenicians and the Roman army; Jesuit Ksara (1857) and Tourelles (1868) began modern production.
regions.terroir: 900 to 1,200 metres; limestone, clay and gravel; dry summers and cold winters.
regions.grapes: Cinsault, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Carignan, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Obaideh, Chardonnay.

regions.name: Batroun
regions.tagline: Coastal mountains north of Byblos, Lebanon's second wine area.
regions.summary: The Batroun hills behind the coast grow vines from near sea level up to around 1,000 metres; Ixsir (in Basbina), Domaine de Baal's sister estates, Atibaia and others have made it Lebanon's most dynamic region outside the Bekaa.
regions.history: A historic wine area near Byblos, revived since the 2000s.

regions.name: Mount Lebanon
regions.tagline: High terraces and the native Merwah.
regions.summary: Scattered high vineyards in Kesrouan, the Chouf and Jezzine, often old terraces of Merwah and Obaideh; Château Musar's winery stands at Ghazir in Kesrouan, though its grapes come mostly from the Bekaa.
regions.history: Christian villages kept winemaking alive under Ottoman rule.

sites.name: Château Musar
sites.text: Gaston Hochar's winery, founded in 1930 in an eighteenth-century castle at Ghazir above Jounieh Bay. Grapes travel from Bekaa vineyards over the mountains; the red (Cabernet Sauvignon, Cinsault, Carignan) is released after about seven years and the white is old-vine Obaideh and Merwah. Serge Hochar's 'natural' approach and its long-lived, variable vintages made it a cult wine.

sites.name: Château Ksara
sites.text: Lebanon's oldest and largest winery, founded by Jesuit priests in 1857 near Zahlé. In 1898 the Jesuits found Roman-era caves, now about two kilometres of cellars at constant temperature; the Vatican told the order to sell in 1972, and a Lebanese consortium bought it. About 3 million bottles a year.

sites.name: Château Kefraya
sites.text: An estate in the West Bekaa on the slopes of Mount Barouk, founded as a winery in 1979 by Michel de Bustros; its Comte de M is one of Lebanon's top reds. During the 1982 invasion its French winemaker was arrested as a spy until he proved he made wine.

sites.name: Massaya
sites.text: Founded in 1998 by the brothers Sami and Ramzi Ghosn with partners from Bordeaux and the Rhône (including Vieux Télégraphe's Brunier family), at Tanail in the central Bekaa; famous for its terrace restaurant and Cinsault-based reds.

sites.name: Temple of Bacchus, Baalbek
sites.text: One of the best-preserved Roman temples in the world, built in the second century AD in the sanctuary of Heliopolis at Baalbek; its portal is carved with vines, grape clusters and Bacchic scenes. A UNESCO World Heritage Site at the northern end of the Bekaa wine zone.

sites.name: Byblos
sites.text: One of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in the world, whose wine was shipped to Old Kingdom Egypt.

sites.name: Tell el-Burak Phoenician wine press
sites.text: A seventh-century BC plastered wine press, one of the largest known in the Phoenician world, excavated south of Sidon with traces of nearby vineyards.

sites.name: Château Marsyas
sites.text: The Saadé family's estate in the West Bekaa near Kefraya, making structured Cabernet and Syrah blends.
